  <title>Governor Ferguson appoints Jenifer Chao to serve as Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs Executive Director</title>
  <link>https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-appoints-jenifer-chao-serve-commission-asian-pacific-american-affairs-executive</link>
  <description>Governor Ferguson appoints Jenifer Chao to serve as Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs Executive Director
  <div class="field field--name-field-date field--type-datetime field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Publish Date</div>
              <div class="field__item"><time datetime="2026-10-30T12:00:00Z" class="datetime">October 30, 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>
<span class="field field--name-uid field--type-entity-reference field--label-hidden"><span>Dan.Jackson@GO…</span></span>
<span class="field field--name-created field--type-created field--label-hidden"><time datetime="2026-10-30T14:12:48-07:00" title="Friday, October 30, 2026 - 2:12pm" class="datetime">October 30, 2026 - 2:12pm</time>
</span>

  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-story-body field--type-text-long field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Story Body</div>
              <div class="field__item"><div class="align-right">
  
  
            <div class="field field--name-field-media-image field--type-image field--label-hidden field__item">  <img loading="lazy" src="/sites/default/files/styles/max_325x325/public/2026-10/JeniferChao.jpg?itok=vpxRRcnp" width="255" height="325" alt="Jenifer Chao" class="image-style-max-325x325">


</div>
      
</div>
<p><span><strong>OLYMPIA</strong> – Today Governor Bob Ferguson announced the appointment of Jenifer Chao as executive director of the Washington State Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs. The appointment is effective Nov. 1.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>The Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs (CAPAA) is a state agency tasked with improving the lives of Asian, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander residents in Washington state by ensuring their access to government, business, education and more. The commission includes an advisory board of 12 commissioners who are also appointed by the Governor.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>The commission traces its origins to Gov. Dan Evans, whose 1972 executive order created The Governor’s Asian Advisory Council. Two years later, the Legislature formally created the commission. In 1995, the name was changed to include Pacific Islanders and Native Hawaiians to reflect the broad diversity of the community.</span></p><p><span>Chao brings more than 25 years of experience in public policy, strategic leadership, and managing complex organizations. Most recently, she worked with the Asian Pacific Islander Coalition Advocating Together for Health (APICAT), a grassroots organization rooted in community.</span></p><p><span>“Washington’s vibrant and growing Asian American and Pacific Islander communities are an integral part of our state’s identity,” Governor Ferguson said. “Jenifer Chao’s deep commitment to the community and extensive advocacy experience will be valuable additions to the Commission."</span></p><p><span>“I am honored to serve as the next Executive Director of CAPAA as we enter a new chapter,” Chao said. “As a Mien immigrant who has dedicated the past 27 years to public service, I understand how public policy can impact a community’s ability to thrive. I am excited to partner closely with our commissioners to advance equity for our Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities.”</span></p><p><span>“The Commission is absolutely thrilled to welcome Jenifer to the team,” CAPAA Chair Kendall Kosai said. “Jenifer’s deep understanding of community combined with her experience navigating complex institutional systems, positions her for success as CAPAA undergoes a period of planning and growth. The Commission looks forward to working together to ensure that all Native Hawaii/Pacific Islander and Asian/Asian American communities are represented in our state government.”</span></p><p><span>Chao received a Bachelor of Arts in Communications from the University of Washington. Before joining APICAT, Chao held various leadership roles at the City of Seattle, including Director of the Department of Neighborhoods, where she advanced community-centered governance. Chao began her public service career at Asian Counseling &amp; Referral Service and Neighborhood House and partnered with community coalitions to advance the needs of immigrant, refugee, and historically underserved communities.</span></p><p><span>Nam Nguyen, a former CAPAA commissioner, has served as interim executive director of CAPAA since 2024. He took over for former executive director Toshiko Grace Hasegawa.</span></p><p><span>“I appreciate Nam Nguyen stepping in to lead the Commission during this transition,” Governor Ferguson said. “Thank you, Nam, for your service to the people of Washington state and our Asian, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander communities.”</span></p></div>

  <title>Governor Ferguson creates Health & Human Services Chief Fraud Prevention Officer as part of new fraud-fighting initiative</title>
  <link>https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-creates-health-human-services-chief-fraud-prevention-officer-part-new-fraud</link>
  <description>Governor Ferguson creates Health &amp; Human Services Chief Fraud Prevention Officer as part of new fraud-fighting initiative
  <div class="field field--name-field-date field--type-datetime field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Publish Date</div>
              <div class="field__item"><time datetime="2026-10-27T12:00:00Z" class="datetime">October 27, 2026</time>

<span class="field field--name-uid field--type-entity-reference field--label-hidden"><span>Brionna.Aho@GO…</span></span>
<span class="field field--name-created field--type-created field--label-hidden"><time datetime="2026-10-27T12:10:12-07:00" title="Tuesday, October 27, 2026 - 12:10pm" class="datetime">October 27, 2026 - 12:10pm</time>
</span>

  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-story-body field--type-text-long field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Story Body</div>
              <div class="field__item"><p><em><span>Executive order also creates Public Funds Fraud Prevention &amp; Accountability Workgroup to coordinate agency prevention efforts</span></em></p><p><span><strong>OLYMPIA</strong> – Governor Bob Ferguson today </span><a href="https://governor.wa.gov/sites/default/files/exe_order/26-05%20-%20Fraud%20Prevention%20%26amp%3B%20Accountability%20%28tmp%29.pdf"><span>signed an executive order</span></a><span> creating the state’s first Chief Fraud Prevention Officer and a statewide fraud prevention workgroup to coordinate and expand on the state’s existing fraud prevention efforts.</span></p><p><span>Governor Ferguson also announced upcoming Governor-request legislation expanding the current Medicaid False Claims Act to cover all false claims against Washington state.</span></p><p><span>“Washington takes fraud seriously,” Governor Ferguson said. “As we continue to face challenging state budgets and devastating cuts from the federal government, it is more important than ever to protect every dollar. My executive order unifies our prevention efforts across state government and expands them.”</span></p><p><span>The Chief Fraud Prevention Officer is tasked with strengthening oversight and coordination of fraud prevention, detection, investigation and recovery efforts specifically related to health and human services programs administered by executive cabinet agencies. Those agencies include the state Health Care Authority and the departments of Health, Social &amp; Health Services, Labor &amp; Industries and Children, Youth &amp; Families.</span></p><p><span>The Chief Fraud Prevention Officer will coordinate with these agencies to improve program integrity and protect federal funding. Governor Ferguson intends to implement this work using existing resources.</span></p><p><span>This work is different from the important work of the Washington State Auditor. The Auditor investigates fraud allegations and whistleblower reports, conducts performance audits of state agencies and local governments and provides technical guidance and training.&nbsp;The Chief Fraud Prevention Officer will work in partnership with the Auditor’s Office, and coordinate efforts in the Governor’s health and human services agencies to stop fraud before it happens.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>“A loss of public resources anywhere diminishes the public’s trust in government overall,” said Washington State Auditor Pat McCarthy. “I applaud the governor’s efforts to improve fraud prevention and detection. Earlier this year I created a director-level Special Investigations division because, like the governor, I believe fraud prevention efforts need to be elevated across government.”</span></p><p><span><strong>Public Funds Fraud Prevention &amp; Accountability Workgroup&nbsp;</strong></span></p><p><span>Governor Ferguson’s order also creates the Public Funds Fraud Prevention &amp; Accountability Workgroup comprised of representatives of the Governor’s cabinet agencies to coordinate their efforts, share best practices and expand on successful strategies across state government. It will be co-chaired by the Governor’s Office and the Office of Financial Management (OFM).&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>The workgroup will create a statewide Public Funds Fraud Prevention and Accountability Framework no later than June 30, 2027, to establish a coordinated statewide approach to fraud prevention, detection, reporting and referral, response, recovery and accountability.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>It will also provide recommendations on potential changes to statutes and regulations, enforcement authority, contractor suspension and debarment standards, reporting mechanisms and whistleblower protections.</span></p><p><span>In addition, the workgroup will make recommendations regarding a public-facing accountability dashboard that reports statewide fraud prevention and accountability performance measures, trends, recoveries, corrective actions and implementation progress.</span></p><p><span>The Governor’s executive order also tasks OFM, the Department of Enterprise Services, the Washington State Patrol and the state Criminal Justice Training Commission with developing new fraud prevention trainings for state employees. Those include basic fraud awareness and ethics, more advanced training for employees working specifically in fraud prevention and financial crimes training for investigators. The Executive Order also establishes a workforce pathway to build talent, provide opportunities for advancement for state employees, and keep talent in state government.</span></p><p><span><strong>Governor to propose state False Claims Act&nbsp;</strong></span></p><p><span>In the upcoming legislative session, Governor Ferguson will propose Governor-request legislation expanding the Medicaid False Claims Act to cover all false claims against Washington state. Currently, 25 states have False Claims Acts to protect against false claims against the government. Washington is one of only five that has only a Medicaid False Claims Act.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>False claims include overcharging the government for goods or services, fraudulently seeking a government contract, submitting a false application for a government loan or grant, or otherwise defrauding the government and violators would be liable for up to three times the actual monetary damages the government sustained, plus civil penalties adjusted for inflation per false claim.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>Enforcement would solely be through private individuals through the whistleblower, or “qui tam,” right of action.</span></p><p><span>In this kind of lawsuit, the person who reports the fraud — the relator — is entitled to a percentage of the penalties awarded by the court, and the state receives the rest. An agency would be designated to monitor the progress of these whistleblower lawsuits through the courts to ensure the state receives its share of recoveries.</span></p></div>

  <description>Governor Ferguson celebrates Outstanding Leadership Award recipients
  <div class="field field--name-field-date field--type-datetime field--label-visually_hidden">

<span class="field field--name-uid field--type-entity-reference field--label-hidden"><span>Dan.Jackson@GO…</span></span>
<span class="field field--name-created field--type-created field--label-hidden"><time datetime="2026-10-26T17:25:40-07:00" title="Monday, October 26, 2026 - 5:25pm" class="datetime">October 26, 2026 - 5:25pm</time>

  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-story-body field--type-text-long field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Story Body</div>
              <div class="field__item"><div>
  
  
            <div class="field field--name-field-media-image field--type-image field--label-hidden field__item">  <img loading="lazy" src="/sites/default/files/2026-10/26OustandingLeadership-32.jpg" width="2048" height="1365" alt="2026 Governor's Outstanding Leadership Award winners.">

</div>
      
</div>
<p><span><strong>OLYMPIA</strong> – Governor Bob Ferguson honored 26 dedicated public servants with the Governor’s Outstanding Leadership Awards today at the Governor’s Mansion.</span></p><p><span>The honorees include managers from multiple state agencies, as well as Everett Community College, Washington State University Vancouver and Washington State University’s Elson S. Floyd College of Medicine. The awards were created in 1985 by Governor Booth Gardner.</span></p><p><span>“Washington’s public employees are the backbone of state government,” Governor Ferguson said. “Today’s honorees are just a few examples of our many dedicated state workers. Thank you all for your work for the people of Washington. It’s a privilege to recognize your contributions. I am proud to work alongside you every day.”</span></p><p><span>The Governor’s Outstanding Leadership Awards honor exceptional managers who exemplify excellence in their performance and accomplishments. They demonstrate the leadership competencies that Washington state needs to embed a performance-driven culture and model the values and behaviors that promote a diverse and inclusive workforce.</span></p><p><span><strong>This year’s honorees:</strong></span></p><p><span><strong>Andrew Davis – Office of Insurance Commissioner</strong></span></p><p><span>Andrew Davis is recognized for leading the Office of the Insurance Commissioner’s Consumer Protection Division with empathy, integrity, and strategic vision. He has strengthened consumer education and advocacy, helped resolve complex insurance complaints, and launched disaster-response outreach that delivered immediate support to residents affected by floods. He also expanded resources for Medicare beneficiaries through the Statewide Health Insurance Benefits Advisors program. By sponsoring the agency’s diversity, equity, and inclusion committee and empowering staff to grow, Andrew has built a modern, collaborative division focused on fair, accessible service and meaningful results for Washington consumers.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Angie Hogenson – Office of Financial Management</strong></span></p><p><span>With 35 years of public service, Angie Hogenson is recognized for turning complex ideas into clear strategies that modernize statewide human resources. She revitalized the Human Resources Management Report, launched the HR Compliance Center, and developed the Workday Readiness Portal, improving service, efficiency, and project quality. Angie centers equity, inclusion, and diverse voices in enterprise decisions while mentoring staff and creating a culture of trust and autonomy. During a major reorganization, she expanded and aligned her team, removed barriers, and strengthened collaboration, leaving the organization more innovative, adaptable, and prepared for the future.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Brenda Heilman – Department of Labor &amp; Industries</strong></span></p><p><span>Brenda Heilman is recognized for steady, innovative leadership within one of the nation’s largest workers’ compensation systems. She developed the division’s first strategic plan in more than a decade, established a new risk-management program, and gave more than 1,200 employees stronger channels to share feedback with executive leadership. Brenda also helped create Washington’s light-duty complaint resolution office, which has resolved more than 750 complaints, and led a pilot to improve care for first responders with post-traumatic stress disorder claims. Her thoughtful, transparent approach has strengthened trust, workplace culture, customer service, and long-term system modernization.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Caroline Byrd – Washington Military Department</strong></span></p><p><span>Although Caroline is now working with the Criminal Justice Training Commission, Caroline Byrd is recognized for extraordinary leadership with Washington’s Military Department in preparing our state for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. She organized six statewide subcommittees, created an executive steering framework, and united state agencies, local governments, tribal nations, and public-safety partners around a shared plan. Caroline developed key operational plans that prepared Washington to manage World Cup activities alongside emergencies such as wildfire season. Through inclusive engagement, clear briefings, newsletters, and office hours, she built trust and alignment across complex partnerships. Her work has strengthened readiness for this global event while creating lasting frameworks for statewide resilience.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Christy Curwick Hoff – Environmental Justice Council</strong></span></p><p><span>For more than two decades, Christy Curwick Hoff has advanced equity, anti-racism, and language access across Washington state government. She has brought community voices into evidence-based policy, established culturally and linguistically appropriate service standards, advanced health impact reviews, and helped turn task force recommendations into state law. During the pandemic, she helped develop an enterprise-wide language access plan so more families could receive critical information. Today, she advises the Environmental Justice Council, guiding investments toward communities most affected by climate change. Known for integrity, humility, and strategic vision, Christy builds diverse teams and partnerships, navigates difficult conversations, and creates lasting change through resilience and mentorship.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Cristina Sepe – Attorney General’s Office</strong></span></p><p><span>Since 2024, Cristina Sepe has played a pivotal role in defending Washington’s policies, people, and funding against federal challenges. Her leadership was central to nearly 50 cases filed in 2025, helping protect critical policy goals and billions of dollars in federal funding. Without relying on formal authority, Cristina coordinates large, diverse legal teams across the Attorney General’s Office, state agencies, and partner states. She also strengthens colleagues through coaching, moot courts, and hands-on support. Her legal excellence, resilience, inclusive leadership, and extraordinary commitment have safeguarded Washington’s interests while building a strong culture of collaboration.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Daniella Byrd – Washington Technology Solutions</strong></span></p><p><span>Daniella Byrd is recognized for collaborative, people-centered leadership that has improved statewide technology services and rebuilt trust among agencies. When unreliable systems and rising vendor costs affected staff and customers, she listened closely, validated the operational impacts, and created clear accountability with technical teams and vendors. Her work improved system performance and advanced a shared statewide solution expected to reduce costs and improve usability. By inviting staff to raise concerns and help shape solutions, Daniella strengthens psychological safety, morale, and engagement. Her transparent communication has delivered lasting operational value for agencies and Washington residents.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Danielle Sullivan – Department of Revenue</strong></span></p><p><span>With more than 30 years of agency experience, Danielle Sullivan has strengthened statewide property-tax administration through equitable, communication-focused leadership. She leads a team of 60 and builds genuine partnerships with county assessors, emphasizing accessibility, responsiveness, and consistency. During significant staff turnover, Danielle rebuilt institutional knowledge, strengthened succession planning, and expanded training and support. She also improved public education through the “Understanding Property Tax” video, translated materials, and easier digital access. By fostering listening, mentorship, teamwork, and psychological safety, Danielle has created lasting improvements in organizational culture, customer service, and confidence across the property-tax system.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>David Makin – Washington State University</strong></span></p><p><span>David Makin has advanced transparency and evidence-based decision-making in public safety by creating the Washington State Data Exchange for Public Safety, now used by more than 75 percent of law-enforcement agencies statewide. He transforms complex information into accessible, community-focused tools that strengthen trust and accountability. David also integrates demographic analysis and collaborative research to examine racial differences in policing, while fostering respect, shared ownership, and professional growth within his team. Through strong partnerships with government, law enforcement, and the public, he has overcome participation and policy challenges and delivered lasting improvements for communities across Washington.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Edward Barry – Department of Transportation</strong></span></p><p><span>For more than 30 years at the Washington State Department of Transportation, Ed Barry has demonstrated sustained, customer-first leadership. He guided the Toll Division through rapid expansion, opening new toll points and expressways while maintaining reliable operations and revenue for public benefit. Ed led an educational response to a statewide phishing scam, advanced cost-saving digital billing, and helped develop a low-income toll program that improves access to express lanes. Known for inclusive leadership and strong employee engagement, he builds consensus across staff, legislators, partners, and peer agencies; delivering complex transportation projects that serve customers fairly and effectively.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Garet Studer – Everett Community College</strong></span></p><p><span>For nearly a decade, Garet Studer has transformed Everett Community College athletics through a person-centered focus on student achievement, equity, and holistic development. By turning data into action and uniting administrators with coaching faculty, he helped achieve an exceptional 86 percent student-retention rate and numerous academic honors. Garet secured support to expand participation and tuition assistance for historically underserved students, and created a student leadership council so student voices shape college decisions. Known for humility, transparency, and care, he empowers staff, breaks down silos, and has built a culture where competitive excellence and academic success reinforce one another.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Jacob Cunnington – Department of Transportation</strong></span></p><p><span>Jacob Cunnington is recognized for exemplary leadership during the U.S. 2 Tumwater Canyon emergency repairs following catastrophic flooding. In a demanding, around-the-clock response, his technical expertise, decisive action, and collaboration helped reopen the highway a month ahead of schedule, restoring vital access for residents, businesses, and emergency services. Jacob also prioritized team well-being, mentored new engineers, and adapted his leadership to help staff succeed under pressure. Despite workforce shortages and continual staffing changes, he maintained high standards and strong communication. His balance of accountability, compassion, and technical excellence delivered an exceptional result for the community.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Jane Beyer – Office of Insurance Commissioner</strong></span></p><p><span>Jane Beyer, though now retired is recognized for thoughtful, effective, and consumer-centered leadership in health-insurance policy. She turned complex ideas into legally sound, practical protections while keeping the needs of Washington consumers at the forefront. Jane led efforts to stop balance billing for emergency services, improve insurer recognition and fair reimbursement for tribal clinics, and reduce administrative barriers. She also advanced accessible, multilingual notices and brings diverse perspectives into policy development. Known for sharing knowledge and credit, confronting difficult issues fairly, and supporting colleagues, Jane’s integrity and persistence have produced lasting improvements in consumer protection across Washington.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Jay Baersten – Washington State Historical Society&nbsp;</strong></span></p><p><span>Over the past four years, Jay Baersten has driven the success of Washington’s Semiquincentennial Committee and launched America 250 as a unifying, bipartisan statewide initiative. She built a network of more than 850 partner organizations, expanded access to history and civics education, and secured major media sponsorships and federal funding for local storytelling and participation. Jay created an inclusive framework that elevates diverse voices and connects communities, schools, cultural institutions, legislators, and state agencies. Through thoughtful relationship-building and clear communication, she has established a lasting foundation for civic and cultural engagement across Washington.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Jessica Barr – Employment Security Department</strong></span></p><p><span>Jessica Barr is recognized for clear, consistent, and people-centered leadership that has improved performance across the Employment Security Department. Her region increased veteran referral completion rates, reduced services to ineligible participants, and shared successful strategies statewide. Jessica also organized cross-state collaboration, led the agency’s first Leadership Summit, and made the relocation of WorkSource Everett an accessible, inclusive model for future moves. During crisis recovery, she protected service continuity while supporting staff well-being. Her transparent communication, active listening, and focus on relationships have strengthened teams, elevated customer experience, and created a culture of continuous learning.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>JR Richards – Employment Security Department</strong></span></p><p><span>JR Richards has delivered measurable results through empathetic, person-centered leadership, helping integrate Unemployment Insurance, Paid Leave, and WA Cares into a more seamless service model. By listening first and involving frontline staff in designing solutions, JR reduced resistance, improved engagement, shortened phone wait times, and increased customer satisfaction. She combines data with employee and customer feedback so decisions reflect both outcomes and human impact. JR also embeds equity, accessibility, and psychological safety into daily work, breaks down organizational silos, and develops emerging leaders through leadership academies. Her strategic vision and compassion have strengthened both agency performance and workplace culture.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Lynn Briscoe – Department of Licensing</strong></span></p><p><span>Lynn Briscoe is recognized for establishing and guiding the Department of Licensing’s Tax Discovery Unit, closing enforcement gaps in regulated industries. She drafted the agency legislation, launched the unit, and built partnerships to address unlicensed activity, tax fraud, and compliance violations. Under Lynn’s direction, the unit analyzed and closed thousands of cases, issued millions of dollars in assessments, and improved voluntary compliance through education and outreach. Her balanced approach combines fair enforcement with clear guidance for businesses and individuals. By building consistent processes, supporting staff, and translating complex requirements into action, Lynn created a trusted statewide program that protects public resources.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>MaryLou Shannon – Department of Transportation</strong></span></p><p><span>MaryLou Shannon is recognized for sustained leadership in strategic project delivery, workforce development, and equity at the Washington State Department of Transportation. Overseeing a regional construction program with more than one billion dollars in infrastructure investments, she delivers projects that improve mobility and safety while strengthening organizational culture. MaryLou championed regional diversity efforts, guided the “Road Trip to Belonging” initiative, and sponsored leadership and professional-growth events. Through intentional recruitment, onboarding, succession planning, and employee engagement, she has built a more inclusive and sustainable workforce. Her collaborative leadership has created lasting benefits for employees, partners, and communities across the region.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Melissa McBride – Department of Labor &amp; Industries</strong></span></p><p><span>Melissa McBride leads three statewide programs that strengthen consumer protection, compliance, and fair competition for thousands of Washington professionals and businesses. Her strategic leadership has resolved administrative backlogs, improved service consistency, and advanced bipartisan policy reforms. Melissa also partnered with language-access programs to remove barriers for people pursuing professional certifications, opening pathways to skilled careers. She builds trusted relationships with advisory groups, stakeholders, and community organizations while mentoring and empowering staff at every level. Rising from an entry-level role, Melissa has demonstrated resilience, transparency, and vision—delivering meaningful change for employees, customers, and communities statewide.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Michelle Underwood – Department of Ecology</strong></span></p><p><span>For 35 years in the Department of Ecology’s Hazardous Waste and Toxics Reduction Program, Michelle Underwood has combined rigorous enforcement with compassion and trust. Her leadership recently broke a four-year stalemate, securing a legal cleanup agreement that will restore 10 acres along the Columbia River and protect human health and the environment. Michelle has also improved customer response times, modernized reporting, strengthened statewide compliance, and reduced environmental risk. When her team faced burnout, she advocated for restructuring, mentorship, and stronger support. Her humility, persistence, and commitment to making work more human have strengthened her team, program, and agency.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Praveen Sekhar – Washington State University</strong></span></p><p><span>Dr. Praveen Sekhar is recognized for 15 years of sustained leadership at Washington State University Vancouver, advancing scientific excellence, equitable opportunity, and community impact. He has secured competitive funding for sensor technologies supporting environmental monitoring and first-responder safety, while building research and workforce pathways for Tribal and underrepresented students. A dedicated mentor, Dr. Sekhar guides students toward publication and professional success, supports junior faculty, and expands participation in engineering and STEM programs. Even when facing institutional barriers, he responds with resilience and purpose. His research, mentorship, and inclusive leadership continue to deliver measurable benefits for Washington and beyond.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Radha Nandagopal, MD – Washington State University</strong></span></p><p><span>At Washington State University’s Elson S. Floyd College of Medicine, Dr. Radha Nandagopal, has helped transform infrastructure, admissions, curriculum, and faculty development to build a physician workforce serving communities statewide. She brings equity into both policy and practice by broadening representation in decisions, investing in scholarship endowments, and mentoring learners and colleagues. Radha creates psychological safety, encourages innovation, and removes barriers so others can succeed. During high-stakes efforts such as accreditation and restructuring, her clarity, empathy, and decisiveness strengthened trust and alignment. Her resilient, collaborative leadership has expanded the college’s impact on Washington’s health-care workforce.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Sarah Pittman – Department of Licensing</strong></span></p><p><span>Sarah Pittman is recognized for leading the Department of Licensing’s implementation of Executive Order 25-03 across dozens of professions and license types. She built strong partnerships across divisions, improved data collection, and created shared ownership of a complex review. Sarah went beyond compliance by identifying inefficiencies and training needs, helping cut licensing processing times nearly in half so applicants could begin work sooner. Through customer and staff journey mapping, she made guidance clearer and processes more equitable. Despite outdated systems, limited resources, and staffing shortages, Sarah’s adaptable, empathetic leadership established a stronger foundation for transparent, efficient, and accessible licensing services.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Savanna Navarro Kresse – Attorney General’s Office</strong></span></p><p><span>Savanna Navarro Kresse is recognized for advancing anti-racist and pro-equity practices throughout the Attorney General’s Office. She helps leaders and divisions embed equity into operations, legal services, policy, and communications. As co-lead of the Racial Disparity in Child Welfare workgroup, Savanna developed practical tools and training to help attorneys identify and address bias. She also helped create a Racial Equity Toolkit for criminal investigations and prosecutions. Through statewide partnerships, committee leadership, and constructive support for colleagues, Savanna continues to strengthen agency culture and service delivery. Her steady leadership sustains progress even under challenging external pressures.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Shannon Steketee – Department of Labor &amp; Industries</strong></span></p><p><span>Shannon Steketee is recognized for transforming how millions of people access state services through practical innovation and customer-centered leadership. She engages directly with users and staff to make digital tools more reliable, accessible, and responsive, especially for people navigating complex information. Shannon brings technology, business priorities, and customer experience together, building trust and shared understanding without relying on formal authority. Under her guidance, multiple web applications met accessibility standards ahead of schedule, and she helped lead a major statewide portal transition. By keeping the customer voice at the center, Shannon has reduced barriers and improved digital service across the agency.</span></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span><strong>Tammy Fellin – Department of Labor &amp; Industries</strong></span></p><p><span>For nearly 13 years, Tammy Fellin has transformed legislative work at the Department of Labor and Industries into a cohesive, responsive network drawing on more than 450 professionals. She has helped address about 1,000 constituent questions and contributed to nearly 280 bill amendments. Since 2014, 94 percent of agency-requested bills have become law, including every bill submitted in the past four years. Tammy has strengthened protections for injured, temporary, agricultural, and limited-English-proficiency workers. A trusted mentor and communicator, she makes complex policy accessible, empowers colleagues to participate in the legislative process, and builds bipartisan relationships that deliver results for Washington communities.</span></p></div>

  <title>Washington, Denmark establish formal ties around maritime and industrial expertise </title>
  <link>https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/washington-denmark-establish-formal-ties-around-maritime-and-industrial-expertise</link>
  <description>Washington, Denmark establish formal ties around maritime and industrial expertise 
  <div class="field field--name-field-date field--type-datetime field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Publish Date</div>
              <div class="field__item"><time datetime="2026-10-22T12:00:00Z" class="datetime">October 22, 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>
<span class="field field--name-uid field--type-entity-reference field--label-hidden"><span>Brionna.Aho@GO…</span></span>
<span class="field field--name-created field--type-created field--label-hidden"><time datetime="2026-10-22T14:32:18-07:00" title="Thursday, October 22, 2026 - 2:32pm" class="datetime">October 22, 2026 - 2:32pm</time>
</span>

  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-story-body field--type-text-long field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Story Body</div>
              <div class="field__item"><div>
  
  
            <div class="field field--name-field-media-image field--type-image field--label-hidden field__item">  <img loading="lazy" src="/sites/default/files/2026-10/Denmark%20MOU-30.jpg" width="5547" height="3698" alt="Denmark signing event">

</div>
      
</div>
<p><strong>SEATTLE —&nbsp;</strong>Governor Bob Ferguson and Ambassador Karen Eva Abrahamsen, Deputy Chief of Mission, Embassy of Denmark in the United States established a new era in trade and partnership between Washington and Denmark with the signing of the <a href="https://governor.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/MEMORANDUM%20OF%20UNDERSTANDING%20WA-DK.pdf">first cooperative agreement between the two regions</a>. Photos from the event are <a href="https://ofmwagov.app.box.com/s/chpn4sl1bzzb5l3r394t4qe93gjuyzdt">available here</a>.</p><p>The agreement establishes a framework for cooperation between the State of Washington and the Royal Danish Embassy to advance shared priorities, including:</p><ul type="disc"><li>Industrial decarbonization</li><li>Water efficiency and reuse</li><li>Commercialization of sustainable fuels</li><li>Port development</li><li>Maritime decarbonization</li><li>Circular manufacturing and industrial symbiosis</li></ul><p>This agreement will help drive further technology exchange and innovation, business ties, study and trade missions and more.</p><p>“From maritime technologies to industrial processes, Washington and Denmark have much to learn from each other,” said Governor Ferguson. “This agreement will support our communities, research institutions, and businesses in strengthening relationships with their Danish partners.”<span>&nbsp;</span></p><p><span lang="EN-GB">“With this agreement, Denmark and Washington State are combining their experience and strengths to create new opportunities for industries, ports and local communities,” said Ambassador Karen Eva Abrahamsen, Deputy Chief of Mission, Embassy of Denmark in Washington, D.C. “I look forward to seeing what we will build together.”</span></p><p><span>Denmark is a world leader in vessel electrification. It has world class maritime engineering talent and government backed green shipping initiatives, including the ongoing implementation of a ferry electrification system. Washington state is also in the midst of electrifying both legacy and next-generation ferries. Together, these programs are among the largest ferry electrification projects in the world.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>Industrial symbiosis refers to&nbsp;</span>taking the waste from one industry, such as heat, left-over materials, or wastewater, and using that waste to feed into a neighboring industry<span>. This makes&nbsp;</span>businesses more efficient and lowers costs, creating growth opportunities while helping achieve climate goals.</p><p>Washington was the first state in the U.S. to develop <a href="https://choosewashingtonstate.com/why-washington/our-key-sectors/industrial-symbiosis/">a state-supported Industrial Symbiosis program</a> and is currently the U.S. leader in advancing these techniques. Danish partners have been instrumental in the development of multiple economic projects around the state. Through this partnership and investments managed by the Washington State Department of Commerce, over 25 Washington ports, cities, and counties are pursuing industrial symbiosis as a strategy for sustainable growth and economic opportunity.</p><p>The signing took place at One Ocean Week, a major global oceans conference in Seattle hosted by Washington Maritime Blue.&nbsp;</p></div>
          </div>
</description>

    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Story Body</div>
              <div class="field__item"><h3><em>All public sector unions vote to approve proposed contract updates</em></h3><p><strong>OLYMPIA —</strong> Governor Bob Ferguson offered the following statement regarding the unanimous approval by public employee unions of new employment contracts for 2027-2029.</p><p>Most public sector unions negotiate contracts with the Office of Financial Management, under the Governor’s Office. Once unions reach a tentative agreement with the bargaining team, they present that proposal for a vote, known as ratification.</p><p>Some unions have the ability to go before third-party arbitrators to finalize their contract terms if they cannot reach agreement with the OFM bargaining team. Several chose to do so.</p><p>All the unions that reached a tentative agreement with OFM voted to ratify those contracts. The unions voting to approve new contracts are:</p><ul><li>Washington Federation of State Employees – General Government (WFSE-GG)</li><li>Association of Washington Assistant Attorneys General (WFSE AWAAG)</li><li>Administrative Law Judges (WFSE ALJ)</li><li>Coalition of Unions (Coalition)</li><li>Professional and Technical Employees Local 17 (Protec17)</li><li>Washington Association of Fish and Wildlife Professionals (WAFWP)</li><li>Service Employees International Union Healthcare 1199 NW (SEIU 1199)</li><li>Washington Public Employees Association (WPEA-GG)</li><li>Washington Public Employees Association – Higher Education (WPEA-HE)</li><li>Washington Federation of State Employees – Higher Education (WFSE</li></ul><p>“When I took office, I inherited a $16 billion budget shortfall," Governor Ferguson said. "We scoured the budget for savings, and made billions of dollars in reductions in order to adopt a balanced budget. Last session, we had a $3.3 billion shortfall, and made more reductions to balance our budget.&nbsp;</p><p>“We are making progress on stabilizing our state budget, while also weathering billions of dollars of cuts by the Trump Administration, including the elimination of health care coverage for thousands of Washingtonians. This coming session, we can expect another challenging budget. The details will become clear as we get more information about our revenue and caseload forecasts, but we know it will be significant. One thing is certain: We have more tough choices ahead.</p><p>“Our state employees do critical work, and I respect their contributions. I appreciate the partnership of our state employee unions during challenging financial circumstances."</p></div>

</description>

  <title>Washington, Finland sign cooperative agreement to build economic, innovation partnerships</title>
  <link>https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/washington-finland-sign-cooperative-agreement-build-economic-innovation-partnerships</link>
  <description>Washington, Finland sign cooperative agreement to build economic, innovation partnerships
  <div class="field field--name-field-date field--type-datetime field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Publish Date</div>
              <div class="field__item"><time datetime="2026-10-14T12:00:00Z" class="datetime">October 14, 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>
<span class="field field--name-uid field--type-entity-reference field--label-hidden"><span>aaron.fishbone…</span></span>
<span class="field field--name-created field--type-created field--label-hidden"><time datetime="2026-10-14T15:31:03-07:00" title="Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - 3:31pm" class="datetime">October 14, 2026 - 3:31pm</time>
</span>

  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-story-body field--type-text-long field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Story Body</div>
              <div class="field__item"><p><span>Governor Bob Ferguson and Finland’s Ambassador to the United States, Leena-Kaisa Mikkola, set a new framework to guide collaboration and trade between Washington and Finland. They gathered at the National Nordic Museum in Seattle to sign a joint Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the two regions and launch a new era of partnership on research, academia, innovation and business. This is the first collaborative agreement with a foreign nation Governor Ferguson has signed since taking office in 2025.</span></p><div>
  
  
            <div class="field field--name-field-media-image field--type-image field--label-hidden field__item">  <img loading="lazy" src="/sites/default/files/2026-10/Finland%20MOU-16.jpg" width="5593" height="3729" alt="Governor and Finland's Ambassador to the USA sign MoU">

</div>
      
</div>
<p><span>The agreement lays out specific industries and research areas that will be the focus of ongoing collaboration between Finland and Washington. These include:</span></p><ul type="disc"><li><span>Modern maritime industry safety, efficiency and sustainability;</span></li><li><span>Aerospace and defense innovation;</span></li><li><span>Clean energy generation, transmission and storage;</span></li><li><span>Sustainable forestry, fisheries and water resource management;</span></li><li><span>Sustainable transportation, including sustainable battery development; and</span></li><li><span>Emerging technologies such as quantum technology and Artificial Intelligence.</span></li></ul><p><span>The agreement helps facilitate trade missions, connects small businesses with potential investors and suppliers, and sets priorities for knowledge sharing and policy expertise.</span></p><p><span>For example: Washington state is a global leader in quantum computing research, and Finland is a leader in producing the cryogenic materials needed for quantum computing. The Washington-Finland agreement helps researchers build their supply chain, particularly small research firms who might not otherwise have the resources to locate international suppliers. Finland is currently building the next-generation fleet of U.S. polar icebreaker vessels. Washington serves as the home of the U.S. icebreaking fleet, employing skilled regional civilian maritime expertise that sustains these vessels between deployments. The partnership can help connect those experts to Finnish shipbuilders to share knowledge about ship design and maintenance as they come into U.S. service.</span></p><p><span>“Washington state and Finland are global leaders in developing cutting-edge innovations,” Governor Ferguson said. “Today’s agreement strengthens our ties and helps build connections to create business opportunities, share expertise and expand academic partnerships with our world-class universities. Our partnership is focused on industries that reflect Washington and Finland’s shared values and complementary strengths. I’m committed to building new opportunities for Washington.”</span></p><p><span>“Finland and Washington state share a strong commitment to innovation and sustainable growth,” Leena-Kaisa Mikkola, Ambassador of Finland to the United States. “Our renewed partnership provides a framework for turning that shared commitment into practical cooperation, including in maritime, clean energy, and advanced technologies. Finnish companies such as Nokia (mobile networks), Wärtsilä (marine and energy technologies), KONE (escalators and elevators), Vaisala (weather technologies), and Kemira (water treatment solutions) create jobs in local communities and further strengthen the ties between Finland and Washington. Partnerships at the state level support transatlantic relations, and Finland is pleased to deepen its ties with Washington state to build on the opportunities ahead.”</span></p><p><span>The signing took place yesterday as part of the 2026 Nordic Innovation Summit in Seattle. The Summit is a unique convening of policymakers, business leaders, researchers, innovators, and cultural voices from across the Nordic region, the Arctic, and the Pacific Northwest to explore the future of Arctic cooperation, climate resilience, energy transition, security, health innovation, and emerging technologies. The Nordic Innovation Summit has become an annual event at the museum, itself an indication of the importance of Nordic ties to Washington.</span></p><p><span>The new collaboration expands on a 2021 agreement, which </span><a href="https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fwww.cip.uw.edu%2F2022%2F09%2F24%2Fcip-jevin-west-finland-education-media-literacy%2F%3Futm_medium=email%26utm_source=govdelivery/1/010101a13b762110-95e8246c-1d90-498f-b940-d2d21689bdf5-000000/otW0gTTtqoVYd5C_LhWx1UaOKVKecKgKO6xlzKwPSFM=452"><span>led to a collaboration</span></a><span> between University of Washington and Finnish educators and institutions on media literacy and combating misinformation. It also led to three official delegations from Washington visiting Finland and a </span><a href="https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fwww.king5.com%2Farticle%2Fnews%2Flocal%2Ffinland-president-visiting-washington-state%2F281-640e8ea3-2ead-4f9a-8add-dc8b56a0807e%3Futm_medium=email%26utm_source=govdelivery/1/010101a13b762110-95e8246c-1d90-498f-b940-d2d21689bdf5-000000/tYs4Qf7pfuAUBfqnjXEVUABB0EIJ9kRKyuLDrK6u5ec=452"><span>2023 Presidential delegation from Finland to Washington</span></a><span>. One of those </span><a href="https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fgcc02.safelinks.protection.outlook.com%2F%3Fdata=05%257C02%257CAaron.Fishbone%2540gov.wa.gov%257C30c3c43e2f6b4be8d36708df28938e5e%257C11d0e217264e400a8ba057dcc127d72d%257C0%257C0%257C639274286515684948%257CUnknown%257CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%253D%253D%257C0%257C%257C%257C%26reserved=0%26sdata=yPirrJ3%252ByBHmKPAFaG9LvSm79qIY%252Bq%252BbqL8GhdTfcEY%253D%26url=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.businessfinland.fi%252Fen%252Fwhats-new%252Fpress-releases%252F2024%252Fgiant-forest-industry-delegation-from-north-america%252F%253Futm_medium%253Demail%2526utm_source%253Dgovdelivery%26utm_medium=email%26utm_source=govdelivery/1/010101a13b762110-95e8246c-1d90-498f-b940-d2d21689bdf5-000000/SWE0JW2qrhfMKByhcPARCR1nlbP90wMMA8O1ox0yLvM=452"><span>Washington delegations</span></a><span> explored partnerships in sustainable forestry, forest management, biomass utilization, and innovative wood-based products. The prior agreement led to the President of Finland visiting Washington state, </span><a href="https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fwww.opb.org%2Farticle%2F2023%2F03%2F06%2Ffinland-president-sauli-niinisto-addresses-washington-state-legislature-us-visit-nato-applications%2F%3Futm_medium=email%26utm_source=govdelivery/1/010101a13b762110-95e8246c-1d90-498f-b940-d2d21689bdf5-000000/V9TDbt-_kZEzkOXbW6-n6ABIAjVIdY4HCA1kA9WUjOM=452"><span>delivering the first-ever address by a foreign head of state</span></a><span> to the Washington State Legislature.</span></p><p><span>More pictures from the event can be found </span><a href="https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fofmwagov.box.com%2Fs%2Fdrh6eusyjq5616y5cvswbmdddoxlbzzg%3Futm_medium=email%26utm_source=govdelivery/1/010101a13b762110-95e8246c-1d90-498f-b940-d2d21689bdf5-000000/yVZ_LvDo6A6zDsKbEE_PrDwGfasaJBNJP5cGCf-yEjU=452" target="_blank"><span>here.</span></a></p></div>

</description>

  <title>Governor Ferguson appoints Haley Wolcott Sebens to Skagit County Superior Court</title>
  <link>https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-appoints-haley-wolcott-sebens-skagit-county-superior-court</link>
  <description>Governor Ferguson appoints Haley Wolcott Sebens to Skagit County Superior Court
  <div class="field field--name-field-date field--type-datetime field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Publish Date</div>
              <div class="field__item"><time datetime="2026-10-09T12:00:00Z" class="datetime">October 09, 2026</time>
</div>

<span class="field field--name-uid field--type-entity-reference field--label-hidden"><span>Conall.Anderso…</span></span>
<span class="field field--name-created field--type-created field--label-hidden"><time datetime="2026-10-09T09:15:13-07:00" title="Friday, October 9, 2026 - 9:15am" class="datetime">October 9, 2026 - 9:15am</time>

  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-story-body field--type-text-long field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Story Body</div>
              <div class="field__item"><p><em>Sebens joins Skagit County Bench in first expansion in 20 years</em></p><p><strong>OLYMPIA</strong> – Today Governor Bob Ferguson announced the appointment of Haley Wolcott Sebens to the position of Skagit County Superior Court Judge. Sebens’ appointment, effective January 1, fills the new position created by a <a href="https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fapp.leg.wa.gov%2Fbillsummary%2F%3FBillNumber=5868%26Initiative=false%26Year=2025%26utm_medium=email%26utm_source=govdelivery/1/010101a1216d312b-5234cf43-d342-4e8f-a039-4275d0a9a1a1-000000/JRDzOTjQgbwr4nTUmfAtdAuKL84A5oFhd0Kt0vsoMfg=452" target="_blank" title="https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fapp.leg.wa.gov%2Fbillsummary%2F%3FBillNumber=5868%26Initiative=false%26Year=2025%26utm_medium=email%26utm_source=govdelivery/1/010101a1216d312b-5234cf43-d342-4e8f-a039-4275d0a9a1a1-000000/JRDzOTjQgbwr4nTUmfAtdAuKL84A5oFhd0Kt0vsoMfg=452">law signed by Governor Ferguson</a> earlier this year. This is the first new position added to the Skagit County Superior Court since 2006.</p><p>Sebens is a judicial officer and longtime litigator with over 16 years of legal experience. She has served as a Skagit County Superior Court Commissioner since January 2025. As a Commissioner, she presides over court calendars including domestic and family law, child welfare and dependencies, at-risk youth, guardianship, probate and estate cases. She serves on the Superior Court Judges Association Family and Juvenile Law Committee and the Minor Guardianship Committee.</p><div class="align-right">
  
  
            <div class="field field--name-field-media-image field--type-image field--label-hidden field__item">  <img loading="lazy" src="/sites/default/files/styles/large/public/2026-10/govdelivery%20sebens.png?itok=tC0q375l" width="347" height="480" alt="Photo of Sebens" class="image-style-large">


</div>
      
</div>
<p>“Haley Wolcott Sebens has demonstrated a strong commitment to serving Skagit residents,” Governor Ferguson said. “Her passion, legal expertise and deep knowledge of the Skagit County Superior Court make her an excellent addition to the bench.”</p><p>“I am grateful to Governor Ferguson for this appointment,” Sebens said. “Having spent my entire legal career in Skagit, I am honored to step into this role, and look forward to continued service to our community.”</p><p>Sebens worked in the Skagit County Prosecutor’s Office for over 10 years, including as Senior Deputy Prosecuting Attorney. There, she specialized in felony crimes involving women and children, including domestic violence, and sexual and special assault cases. She led the Skagit County multi-disciplinary team focused on local intra-agency coordination of cases involving child physical and sexual abuse and served on the Skagit County Domestic Violence Task Force. She also handled felony cases including homicides, property crimes, narcotics and felony traffic cases.</p><p>As a trial attorney, Sebens handled over 80 jury trials. She argued and handled cases at the Washington State Court of Appeals and the Washington Supreme Court. Sebens also regularly presented and trained at prosecutor and trial attorney conferences across the state.</p><p>Sebens previously worked as a Skagit County Public Defender handing gross misdemeanor and misdemeanor criminal cases, as well as representing parents involved in the child welfare system.</p><p>Prior to being appointed as Commissioner, Sebens acted as judge pro tem for municipal and district courts including Snohomish District Court, City of Ferndale and City of Lynnwood.</p><p>Sebens is an active member of Burlington Rotary, the Big W Club, Teen Court and the PTA, and a 2024 Leadership Skagit graduate. She regularly mentors youth in the community, facilitating interest in the legal profession.</p><p>Sebens resides in Skagit Valley with her husband and two busy children.</p><p>Sebens earned her bachelor’s degree from the University of Washington and competed for several years as a student-athlete. She graduated from Gonzaga Law School, where she served as an editor of the Gonzaga Law Review.</p></div>
          </div>
</description>

  <title>Governor Ferguson selects 99 Opportunity Zones to encourage private investment </title>
  <link>https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-selects-99-opportunity-zones-encourage-private-investment</link>
  <description>Governor Ferguson selects 99 Opportunity Zones to encourage private investment 
  <div class="field field--name-field-date field--type-datetime field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Publish Date</div>
              <div class="field__item"><time datetime="2026-10-08T12:00:00Z" class="datetime">October 08, 2026</time>
</div>
          </div>
<span class="field field--name-uid field--type-entity-reference field--label-hidden"><span>aaron.fishbone…</span></span>
<span class="field field--name-created field--type-created field--label-hidden"><time datetime="2026-10-08T09:46:20-07:00" title="Thursday, October 8, 2026 - 9:46am" class="datetime">October 8, 2026 - 9:46am</time>
</span>

  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-story-body field--type-text-long field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Story Body</div>
              <div class="field__item"><p><em><span>Federal program connects private capital with low-income communities</span></em></p><p><span><strong>OLYMPIA —&nbsp;</strong>Today Governor Bob Ferguson announced the nominations of 99 low-income and rural communities across Washington state for the federal Opportunity Zones 2.0 program.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>The second-generation program encourages investors, developers and financial institutions to fund real estate development and businesses in exchange for tax incentives. The first generation of the program spurred an estimated $100 billion in private investments nationwide.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>Gov. Ferguson submitted the nominations, representing 27 counties and 17 tribal lands, to the U.S. Treasury Department. The new designations will take effect January 1, 2027. View the full list of nominations and program details on the&nbsp;</span><a href="https://commercehub.maps.arcgis.com/apps/dashboards/8646d648e13347d48bd0792026cb9582"><span>Summary OZ Dashboard</span></a>.<span>&nbsp;</span></p><p><span>“Washington is a great place to do business,” Governor Ferguson said. “Opportunity Zones help shine a light on communities that have exceptional potential for investors.”</span></p><p><span>In 2018, 139 areas across 36 counties were nominated for the first-generation version of this program. When the updated program was announced in 2025, the state created a plan to engage with the public and transparently evaluate applications. Feedback received helped finalize the criteria and the application forms used for the next round of nominations.</span></p><p><span>The public, business leaders and the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes participated in months of feedback and strategic planning, led by the Washington State Department of Commerce.</span></p><p><span>“We started by listening to communities about their strengths, their ambitions, and what they need to grow,” said Sarah Clifthorne, Interim Director, Washington State Department of Commerce. “There is immense untapped potential across Washington for private investments to thrive and unlock the next chapter of growth. Our goal is to encourage that partnership with local people and the variety of spaces ready for impact.”</span></p><p><span>The 99 nominated areas were selected from 152 applications. Of those, 36 represent opportunities in rural communities.</span></p><p><span><strong>How the program works</strong></span></p><p><span>Originally launched in 2018, the federal program spurred more private investment across economically distressed communities than any previous policy over a comparable period nationally. Investments tied to that first round of designations are estimated to have surpassed $100 billion, reaching over 5,600 neighborhoods nationwide.</span></p><p><span>In the announced update to the program in 2025, Congress added strict information reporting requirements designed to measure long-term economic impacts. Active funds operating within the original 2018 Opportunity Zones must now adhere to these new compliance mandates.</span></p><p><span>Meanwhile, geographic designations under the initial OZ 1.0 framework will remain active through Dec. 31, 2028, overlapping with the launch of the updated program.</span></p><p><span>This impacts several projects underway in Washington state. For example, the Peyton Lofts development in Spokane is looking to add residential density to the urban core, transforming a 135-year-old office building into a&nbsp;96-unit mixed-use residential community&nbsp;by the end of 2027. It represents a growing effort across the state to turn empty commercial offices into residences at a time when housing is critically needed.</span></p><p><span>Notable completed projects also include:</span></p><ul type="disc"><li><span>The Koz on MLK affordable and workforce housing development in Tacoma’s Hilltop Neighborhood. Backed by an initial 2018 investment framework, a&nbsp;woman-owned developer&nbsp;finished the building in 2022. It now houses 161 units and ground-floor commercial spaces.</span><br>&nbsp;</li><li><span>The Marina Square mixed-use waterfront development in Bremerton completed in 2023 on the site of a former parking lot. Today, it features 270 residential units and nearly 13,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, anchored by the Market at Marina Square and an Express YMCA facility.&nbsp;It now supports the city’s broader waterfront revitalization plans.</span></li></ul><p><span><strong>What’s new in Opportunity Zones 2.0</strong></span></p><p><span>The new Opportunity Zone program adds new incentives targeted directly at high-need rural communities:</span></p><ul type="disc"><li><span>Investors who hold a Qualified Rural Opportunity Fund (QROF) investment for five years receive a 30% reduction in taxable value, compared to 10% for the same holding period in non-rural zones.</span></li><li><span>Rural properties require capital improvements equal to only 50% of their adjusted basis to qualify for tax benefits, down from the standard 100% threshold.</span></li><li><span>Once certified, a designated Opportunity Zone 2.0 area will keep its status through Dec. 31, 2036.&nbsp;</span></li><li><span>The 2.0 program is built on a permanent, recurring 10-year cycle, so newly drawn maps will take over on Jan. 1, 2037.</span></li><li><span>The new IRS information reporting requirements allow for&nbsp;the program’s successes&nbsp;and challenges to be measured accurately. Currently, it is unclear how many specific jobs or investment resulted from OZ 1.0, and the new requirement will improve transparency</span></li></ul><p><span><strong>What happens next</strong></span></p><p><span>The U.S. Treasury Department will review and certify all nominations it receives from states after submission. Designations are scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.</span></p><p><span>Investors can register their Qualified Opportunity Funds (QOFs) with the IRS and begin auditing their realized 2026 capital gains now by visiting&nbsp;</span><a href="https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/businesses/invest-in-a-qualified-opportunity-fund"><span>irs.gov/credits-deductions/businesses/invest-in-a-qualified-opportunity-fund</span></a><span>.</span></p><p><span>Demand for sites within the new boundaries is also expected to be high. The Department of Commerce encourages investors to prepare their strategies ahead of January 1 so they can deploy capital early in 2027 and immediately drive community impact.</span></p></div>

              <div class="field__item"><div class="SCXW89442061 BCX8"><div class="OutlineElement Ltr SCXW89442061 BCX8"><p class="Paragraph SCXW89442061 BCX8" lang="EN-US"><em><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">New application brings total request for federal Public Assistance over $133M</span></em><span class="EOP Selected SCXW89442061 BCX8">&nbsp;</span></p></div><div class="OutlineElement Ltr SCXW89442061 BCX8"><p class="Paragraph SCXW89442061 BCX8"><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US"><strong>OLYMPIA —</strong> Governor Ferguson submitted </span><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun ContextualSpellingAndGrammarErrorV2Themed" lang="EN-US">an</span><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US"> </span><a href="https://governor.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/Major-Disaster-Declaration-Request-Addendum_2026_WildFires_CAO-0930206_final.pdf" target="_blank"><span class="TextRun Underlined SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">additional request to the Federal Emergency Management Agency for Public Assistance</span></a><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US"> funding to help repair state infrastructure damaged by the devastating wildfires in Central and Eastern Washington. This brings the total amount of federal Public Assistance Washington has requested for this disaster to over $133 million.</span><span class="EOP Selected SCXW89442061 BCX8">&nbsp;</span></p></div><div class="OutlineElement Ltr SCXW89442061 BCX8"><p class="Paragraph SCXW89442061 BCX8"><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">In late July and early August 2026, multiple huge wildfires raged through Central and Eastern Washington. The fires destroyed hundreds of homes, forced mass evacuations from homes and hospitals, caused widespread power outages, disrupted essential services, and caused long-term damage to ranching and agricultural businesses in rural communities. Dozens of our heroic firefighters were injured in the line of duty. The damage left in the fires’ wake continues to overwhelm state, local, Tribal, nonprofit, and private-sector capabilities.</span><span class="EOP Selected SCXW89442061 BCX8">&nbsp;</span></p></div><div class="OutlineElement Ltr SCXW89442061 BCX8"><p class="Paragraph SCXW89442061 BCX8" lang="EN-US"><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">“Federal assistance is essential to our state’s recovery from these historic wildfires,” Governor Ferguson said. “My team and I are laser-focused on helping people recover from this disaster.”</span><span class="EOP Selected SCXW89442061 BCX8">&nbsp;</span></p></div><div class="OutlineElement Ltr SCXW89442061 BCX8"><p class="Paragraph SCXW89442061 BCX8"><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">Governor Ferguson </span><a href="https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-requests-federal-major-disaster-declaration-four-counties-additional-state-level" target="_blank"><span class="TextRun Underlined SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">previously submitted a request for a federal Major Disaster Declaration</span></a><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">, which is critical to unlocking federal dollars to assist in Washington’s recovery. At that time, Governor Ferguson also requested FEMA Individual Assistance for homeowners, and two types of Public Assistance — clearing </span><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun ContextualSpellingAndGrammarErrorV2Themed" lang="EN-US">debris, and</span><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US"> recovering costs from the emergency response. This new application seeks additional </span><a href="https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/2020-07/fema_public-assistance-fact-sheet_10-2019.pdf" target="_blank"><span class="TextRun Underlined SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">Public Assistance for permanent repairs to public infrastructure</span></a><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">.&nbsp;</span><span class="EOP Selected SCXW89442061 BCX8">&nbsp;</span></p></div><div class="OutlineElement Ltr SCXW89442061 BCX8"><p class="Paragraph SCXW89442061 BCX8"><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">FEMA’s Public Assistance Program provides up to 75% reimbursement by the federal government for qualifying repairs to our infrastructure. That includes the cost of removing debris, as well as repairing damage to roads, bridges, public buildings, public utilities, water control facilities, parks, and more.</span><span class="EOP Selected SCXW89442061 BCX8">&nbsp;</span></p></div><div class="OutlineElement Ltr SCXW89442061 BCX8"><p class="Paragraph SCXW89442061 BCX8"><span class="TextRun SCXW89442061 BCX8 NormalTextRun" lang="EN-US">The new request seeks additional Public Assistance to Asotin, Chelan, Columbia, Douglas, Ferry, Grant, Okanogan, Spokane, Stevens, Whitman, and Yakima Counties, as well as the Spokane Tribe of Indians.&nbsp;</span><span class="EOP Selected SCXW89442061 BCX8">&nbsp;</span></p></div><div class="OutlineElement Ltr SCXW89442061 BCX8"><p class="Paragraph SCXW89442061 BCX8"><span   <title>Governor Ferguson launches Phone-Free Schools Act at Spokane event</title>
  <link>https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-launches-phone-free-schools-act-spokane-event</link>
  <description>Governor Ferguson launches Phone-Free Schools Act at Spokane event
  <div class="field field--name-field-date field--type-datetime field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Publish Date</div>
              <div class="field__item"><time datetime="2026-10-02T12:00:00Z" class="datetime">October 02, 2026</time>

<span class="field field--name-uid field--type-entity-reference field--label-hidden"><span>Conall.Anderso…</span></span>
<span class="field field--name-created field--type-created field--label-hidden"><time datetime="2026-10-06T15:23:51-07:00" title="Tuesday, October 6, 2026 - 3:23pm" class="datetime">October 6, 2026 - 3:23pm</time>
